query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The introduction of a controlled amount of oxygen and nitrogen interstitials, within the range of 1 to 3 atomic %, can improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: Titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy in the as-cast or homogenized condition
generation.intervention: Introduction of oxygen and nitrogen interstitials at trace levels (1 to 3 atomic %)
generation.conditions: Elevated temperatures, potentially up to 900°C, and long-term service conditions
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of α-Ti precipitates with solid solution oxygen and nitrogen
generation.mechanism: Solid solution strengthening and potential phase stability effects due to interstitials
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved high-temperature strength and room-temperature ductility compared to the alloy without the intervention
generation.baseline: Mechanical properties of the alloy without oxygen and nitrogen interstitials
generation.boundary: Operating temperatures up to 900°C and service durations potentially exceeding 40 days
generation.uncertainty: Long-term stability and potential phase segregation effects at in-service temperatures

falsification_experiment.design: Thermal aging and nanoindentation experiments on titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloys with and without controlled oxygen and nitrogen interstitials
measurements: Microstructure evolution using HAADF-STEM, EDX, APT, and EELS
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the introduction of oxygen and nitrogen interstitials does not lead to improved mechanical properties or if the precipitates formed are not α-Ti with solid solution oxygen and nitrogen, the hypothesis is falsified.

Equimolar Ti-V-Nb-Ta has an extremely high compressive yield strength, 1273 MPa at room temperature and 688 MPa at 900°C (). By comparison, conventional high-temperature Ni-base superalloys notably soften above 600°C, with the compressive yield strength dropping to ~200 MPa at 900°C (). Equimolar Ti-V-Nb-Ta also exhibits impressive tensile ductility, ~14% at room temperature (), and a relatively low brittle-to-ductile transition temperature between −47° and −27°C, comparable to BCC metals and stainless steels for engineering applications (, ).
Despite these advances, the bulk of experimental work studying the Ti-V-Nb-Ta system and other RHEAs has focused on materials under the as-cast or homogenized conditions. These conditions may not accurately represent their long-term structural/mechanical stability at service temperatures. As a newly developed material system, a comprehensive understanding of their long-term stability under potential service temperatures remains to be established. In the present investigation, Ti-V-Nb-Ta samples were subjected to thermal aging for various durations at 700°C. The microstructure and mechanical properties of Ti-V-Nb-Ta before and after thermal aging were revealed by a combination of state-of-the-art microstructural characterization and nanoindentation techniques. Results indicate that impurity interstitials at the trace levels within the solid solution encourage the formation of α-Ti precipitates in the Ti-V-Nb-Ta alloy when aged at high temperature, which undermines the effects of interstitial solid solution strengthening and leads to softening.
